analysis.one_liner: Requires retirement plan managers to pick investments only on financial returns, not social or environmental goals.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. Daines with 1 Republican cosponsor, the bill never received a Senate vote and died in committee when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal retirement law (ERISA) to require anyone managing a worker retirement plan to choose investments based only on factors that affect financial risk and return. Managers could weigh social or environmental goals only in narrow cases, such as when two investments are financially indistinguishable, and could not put ESG-style funds in a plan's automatic default investment. The bill never got a hearing or vote; it sat in the Senate committee that handles labor law until Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose plan managers would otherwise have weighed environmental or social goals, and who want investments picked purely on expected returns. It also indirectly benefits industries that ESG funds avoid or pressure — companies whose stock some retirement funds decline to hold or whose behavior those funds push to change, such as fossil fuel producers.

how_it_helps.text: Requires fiduciaries to select and maintain plan investments based solely on pecuniary factors — factors expected to materially affect the investment's risk or return [S2][S3].

Allows non-pecuniary factors only when a fiduciary cannot distinguish between investments financially (with documented justification), or when participants in a defined contribution plan choose from a broad menu of options — and even then, ESG funds may not be a plan's qualified default investment [S2][S3].
Supporters present this as protecting workers' retirement savings from investment decisions driven by goals other than returns [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who would want their retirement money in funds that consider environmental, social, or governance factors: the plan could not use such a fund as the default, and a manager could almost never choose one on its own judgment. Managers of ESG-style funds would lose potential placement in retirement plans' default options.

drawbacks.text: The bill bars ESG-style funds from serving as a plan's default investment and sharply limits a fiduciary's ability to choose them, even for participants who would prefer them; workers wanting such options would have to actively opt in from the plan's menu [S2][S3].

The rule works in only one direction: it restricts environmental and social factors but does not restrict investing on the basis of opposing non-financial preferences, and it rewrites established fiduciary practice based on a claim — that ESG factors reduce returns — that the bill itself does not establish [S3].

Requiring managers to ignore any factor not defined as strictly financial could prevent plans from considering risks that many analysts do treat as financially material over long horizons, such as long-term climate exposure [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is ideological and indirect: nothing in the bill is shown to raise typical returns, since factors expected to materially affect risk and return remain permissible. The main real-world effect is to keep environmental and social funds out of retirement plan defaults and narrow managers' discretion, at the cost of choice for workers who want their savings invested differently. As a worker-protection measure, the gains are modest and unproven.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Steve Daines introduced the bill on June 23, 2022, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1][S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — is recorded for the remainder of the Congress [S5].
The bill attracted one cosponsor, a Senate Republican [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers' plan managers keep their existing discretion to weigh ESG factors, and ESG-style funds keep access to the retirement market, including default options that the bill would have barred them from.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: ESG fund managers keep market access

for.name: Sen. Steve Daines
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restrict retirement plan investment decisions to pecuniary factors.

against.name: Patty Murray
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration, leaving it without a hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator sponsored the bill and it drew one Republican cosponsor; with Democrats holding the Senate and the HELP Committee chairmanship, no Democrat supported it and the committee took no action [S4][S5].

industries.note: ESG and climate-aware funds decline to hold, or pressure, fossil fuel securities; the bill limits retirement plans' ability to weight those factors, reducing the risk that trillions in worker retirement money shifts away from the industry. Workers gain nothing demonstrated; the industry's investor base is protected.

The bill would bar ESG-style funds from a plan's default investment and nearly eliminate a fiduciary choosing one on its own, shrinking their place in the retirement market; their death with the bill preserved that market.

industries.industry: Retirement plan fiduciaries and asset managers
industries.note: The bill imposes a strict pecuniary-only mandate and documentation requirements, narrowing managers' discretion, but it also shields managers from pressure to offer ESG defaults and codifies bright-line rules that reduce litigation ambiguity.
